# Why this pattern matters

`reusable-footnotes` is motivated by a citation pattern that is especially common in **Law**. Legal scholarship, briefs, opinions, memoranda, and books often place bibliographic references in page footnotes rather than relying only on a final reference list.

The same pattern is also familiar in **History, Philosophy, Theology, Classics, literary studies, and other Humanities disciplines**, where full references in footnotes keep documentary support close to the argument.

The important distinction is between the **bibliographic source** and the **footnote occurrence**. BibTeX should define the source once; Quarto should decide how that source is rendered where it is cited.

# Two native Quarto citation forms

A normal Pandoc/Quarto citation remains completely unchanged:

```qmd
A normal citation stays normal: [@barroso2024].
```

For example: a normal citation stays normal [@barroso2024].

The vendored `bibentry` extension adds a second, explicit representation:

```qmd
[@barroso2024]{.bibentry}
```

That form prints the **full bibliography entry using the bibliography layout of the active CSL style**. It does not redefine what `@barroso2024` means.

Here is the full entry inline:

[@barroso2024]{.bibentry}

If the document defines, for example,

```yaml
bibliography: references.bib
csl: your-style.csl
```

then both the ordinary citation and the `.bibentry` representation use the same bibliography database and the same CSL configuration. The ordinary citation uses the CSL citation layout; `.bibentry` extracts the corresponding bibliography-layout entry.

# Legal-style footnotes

The useful composition is entirely native Pandoc syntax:

```qmd
A legal proposition.^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}]
```

Rendered here:

A constitutional proposition may be supported in a page footnote.^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}]

This is the core legal use case: the prose contains only a superscript marker, while the footnote contains the full bibliographic entry.

A second authority works the same way.^[See [@mendes2023]{.bibentry}]

The mechanism is not limited to Law. A historical argument can use the same pattern.^[See [@bloch1953]{.bibentry}]

# Reusing the same bibliographic footnote

`bibentry` and `reusable-footnotes` have separate responsibilities:

- **`bibentry`** resolves a citation key and prints its long CSL bibliography form;
- **`reusable-footnotes`** controls recurrence of identical footnote content.

Because `bibentry` runs first, two identical bibliographic footnotes become identical footnote AST content before `reusable-footnotes` evaluates them.

For example, this reference appears once here.^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}]

And the same reference appears again later with exactly the same footnote content.^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}]

Within the current reusable-footnote scope, both occurrences can point to the same canonical note instead of duplicating the same long reference text.

If the footnote content changes, it is treated as a different note. This makes locators explicit and predictable:

```qmd
A proposition.^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}, p. 185.]

Another proposition.^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}, p. 241.]
```

The different locator text makes those footnotes distinct.

# True inline replacement

The modified `bibentry` implementation replaces only the marked citation span, not the surrounding paragraph.

```qmd
For publication details, see [@barroso2024]{.bibentry} and compare the discussion above.
```

Rendered:

For publication details, see [@barroso2024]{.bibentry} and compare the discussion above.

This is important because the upstream prototype originally operated mainly at paragraph level. The extended implementation walks the AST recursively, so it also works inside nested structures such as native footnotes.

# Why BibTeX remains the source of truth

The author should not copy and paste formatted references into `^[...]`. Instead, the `.bib` entry provides the stable identity:

```bibtex
@book{barroso2024,
  author    = {Barroso, Luís Roberto},
  title     = {Curso de direito constitucional contemporâneo},
  edition   = {12},
  address   = {São Paulo},
  publisher = {Saraiva},
  year      = {2024}
}
```

The document can then choose between two representations without duplicating data:

```qmd
Normal citation: [@barroso2024]

Full entry: [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}

Full entry in a footnote: ^[See [@barroso2024]{.bibentry}]
```

# Current integration

This repository currently vendors an **extended development version** of Fred Guth's [`bibentry`](https://github.com/fredguth/bibentry) extension under `_extensions/bibentry/` for integration testing. The original project is MIT licensed and remains credited to Frederico Guth.

The proposed upstream changes add:

- recursive AST support, including `.bibentry` inside footnotes;
- true inline replacement without replacing the whole paragraph;
- one citeproc pass over the full document, preserving bibliography ordering and numeric styles;
- bibliography preservation through `nocite` rather than hidden CSS/Typst content;
- HTML, PDF/LaTeX, DOCX, and Typst-compatible AST output.

The intention is to propose these changes back to `fredguth/bibentry` rather than permanently maintain a competing bibliography-rendering extension here.

# Output formats

The integration is designed to remain writer-neutral:

| Format | `bibentry` inside a native footnote | Reusable identical note |
|---|---|---|
| HTML | native footnote with full CSL entry | canonical note within the rendered page |
| PDF | native LaTeX footnote with full CSL entry | repeated clickable marker |
| DOCX | native Word footnote with full CSL entry | canonical note within the configured DOCX scope |

No Python or output-specific post-processing is required.
